messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Linh Nguyen is a 51-year-old dentist who came to treatment after more than a year of living as if danger were always about to step back into the room. The trouble began after a former patient started contacting the office repeatedly after a routine course of treatment. At first the messages were framed as compliments and requests to see her again, but they became increasingly intrusive, appearing across the clinic phone, her work email, and social media. He waited outside the dental building at closing time on several occasions, once standing near her car and smiling as though he had every right to be there. On another evening, as she hurried out after seeing her last patient, music from a nearby parked car was playing the same love song he had mentioned in one of his messages. She remembered the way he looked at her then, calm and certain, while she felt trapped in the open parking lot with no clear place to go. Police were contacted after he followed her for part of her drive home, but even after a report was filed, Linh did not experience their involvement as restoring safety. The fact that he had already crossed so many boundaries made the world feel porous to her, as if protection was more theoretical than real.

In the months that followed, what unsettled her most was how ordinary moments could suddenly fill with the same sense of exposure. Certain songs were especially potent. If one came on in a grocery store or drifted from a patient’s phone in the waiting room, she felt her body tense before she had fully registered why. Related media content had a similar effect; news stories or television scenes about stalking, harassment, or women being watched could leave her scanning the room and replaying the sense that no one recognizes danger until it is already too late. Even the presence of police could make her more uneasy rather than reassured. Seeing an officer near the hospital parking structure next to her practice, or noticing a patrol car outside, brought back the period when reports had been made and nothing in her lived experience had changed quickly enough to feel protective. In those moments she became certain that other people’s assurances were irrelevant. Even if her husband told her she was safe, or a colleague reminded her that the office had security cameras, she could not make herself believe it.

That conviction shaped the way she moved through her days. At the dental practice, Linh began choosing seats in the staff lounge only if she could watch the doorway. In consultations, if there was any choice in where to sit, she positioned herself so her back was against a wall and she could see the room. At restaurants she quietly steered her husband toward tables along the perimeter, and in continuing education seminars she arrived early enough to claim a place near an exit but still with a solid wall behind her. She described this not as preference but necessity: if she sat exposed in the middle of a room, she could not follow conversation because too much of her attention was fixed on who might approach from behind. The same logic governed where she parked at work and how long she lingered after her last patient. Safety had become, in her mind, something she had to engineer moment by moment because it could not be trusted to exist on its own.

As this pattern hardened, her world grew narrower and more effortful. In the operatory she remained highly professional, but she noticed herself tracking sounds in the hallway and feeling a surge of vigilance whenever unfamiliar male voices entered reception. When patients left music playing on their phones, she found herself listening for particular songs rather than concentrating fully on charting. At home, if a film trailer or news segment touched on stalking, the rest of the evening could be colored by the feeling that she needed to check locks again and reconsider where she would sit in the living room. Her husband had become used to the way she scanned restaurants before committing to a seat, though she felt ashamed that she could no longer accept his reassurance as comforting.

What finally brought Linh to seek help was not a new assault, but the dawning realization that she had organized nearly every environment around anticipated danger and still never felt safe. A song playing unexpectedly in a café near her office recently left her so shaken that she abandoned lunch and returned to the clinic early, only to spend the afternoon distracted and on edge. She said she is frightened that this is how her life will remain: always calculating sightlines, always unconvinced by reassurance, always one reminder away from feeling exposed again. What she hopes for, carefully and a little skeptically, is not to forget what happened but to stop living as though the stalker still has access to every room she enters.
